_comment: Shared contract for the tax and option calculations.
These five calculations are implemented TWICE and independently: in Python
(backend/parity_tools.py, used by the web app through /api/tools/tax/*) and in Kotlin
(android-app/.../OfflineRepository.kt, used by the phone when it runs offline). Nothing
compared them, so they drifted — see the `divergence` notes below, every one of which was
Python is the reference: it is the implementation the web app actually runs, and it models
the treaty credit cap and configurable rates that the Kotlin side dropped. Expected values
here were generated by calling the Python functions, not by hand.
Amounts are compared to 2 decimal places, option prices to 4. Fields absent from a case's
`expect` block are not part of the contract; `generatedAt` is always ignored.
Read by tests/test_tax_spec.py. The Kotlin half is not wired up yet.

cases.why: 30% withheld abroad but the treaty only credits 15%, so 4% is still due in Poland.
Omitting the Polish rate and the treaty cap must fall back to 19% and 15%.
cases.divergence: Kotlin reads localTaxPct as 0 when absent, so it reports no Polish tax due.

cases.why: Carry-forward loss reduces the base before the rate is applied.
The rate is an input, not a constant.
cases.divergence: Kotlin hardcodes 0.19 and ignores taxRatePct entirely.

cases.why: No rate given means the statutory 19%.
Same treaty cap as dividends: only 15% of the 30% withheld abroad is creditable.
cases.divergence: Kotlin credits the full foreign withholding and has no cap, so it under-reports the Polish tax due.

cases.why: Coupon plus discount gain minus costs, taxed at the given rate.
No rate given means the statutory 19%.
cases.divergence: Kotlin uses the raw value, so an absent rate yields zero tax.

cases.why: An options contract covers 100 units unless stated otherwise.
cases.divergence: Kotlin defaults the multiplier to 1, making position P/L 100x too small.

cases.why: Puts gain as spot falls below strike; P/L scales with contracts.
Spot equal to strike is ATM, and the whole premium is time value.
cases.divergence: Kotlin knows only ITM and OTM, and returns Polish prose instead of a machine-readable recommendation.

cases.why: Loss harvesting takes the biggest unrealised loss first and stops once the base reaches zero.
cases.divergence: Kotlin does no harvesting at all: it returns taxSaved 0 and an empty action list, so the phone always reports that nothing can be saved.
